title: Annotatio IV §.IV close: 1 Cor. 11 — Institution tropes; two things celestial & terrestrial; stop before §.V
pass_a_gloss: The latter or Eleventh chapter to the Corinthians serves chiefly to found the true Sentence concerning the Sacred Supper in that Paul there repeats from Christ’s mouth the Institution words with a certain emphatic interpretation, whereby he greets the bread not simply as Christ’s Body but as the body broken for us (v. 24); and the Cup, or wine in the cup, not simply as Christ’s blood but as that New covenant through His blood (v. 25) — thereby declaring most lucidly that the Sacramental Propositions are improper or tropical, meanwhile by no means denying spiritual presence and participation of Christ’s body and flesh — and in the three verses immediately following 26–28, about to teach that the Sacrament of the Sacred Supper consists of two things, celestial and terrestrial, no less after than before the words commonly called consecration, and that neither is converted or transmuted into the other’s substance, i.e. bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, he more often doubles bread and cup, saying: As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup &c. Therefore whoever shall eat this bread unworthily &c. But let a man examine himself and so eat of this bread. &c.
pass_b_english: 1 Cor. 11 chiefly founds the true Supper sentence: Paul repeats Institution from Christ’s mouth with emphasis — bread as body broken for us (v. 24); cup as the New covenant through His blood (v. 25) — tropical propositions, without denying spiritual presence and participation.
Vv. 26–28: the sacrament is two things, celestial and terrestrial, after consecration as before — bread and wine are not converted into body and blood; he keeps saying this bread / this cup.
Stop before §.V (Pauline true sentence lasting through the Apostolic first age).
source_text: Posterius seu Undecimum ad Corinthios caput Pauli, eatenus potissimum veræ Sententiæ de S. Cœna fundandæ inservit, quòd Paulus in eo, ex ore Christi, Institutionis verba, idque cum emphatica quâdam interpretatione repetit, quâ & panem non simpliciter Corpus Christi, sed corpus pro nobis fractum vers. 24.; Poculum verò, seu vinum in poculo, non simpliciter sanguinem Christi, sed Novum illud pactum per sanguinem suum vers. 25. salutat (hôc pacto Propositiones Sacramentales improprias seu tropicas luculentissimo modo declarans, præsentiam interim ac participationem, tam corporis, quàm carnis Christi spiritualem, neutiquam inficiatus) in sequentibus immediatè versiculis tribus 26. 27. & 28., Sacramentum S. Cœnæ ex duabus rebus, cœlesti & terrestri, non minus, post, quàm ante consecrationis dicta vulgò verba, constare, nec harum alteram in alterius substantiam i. e. panem & vinum in corpus & sanguinem Christi, converti aut transmutari edocturus, panem crebriùs & poculum ingeminat, dicens: Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc & poculum hoc biberitis &c. Itaque quisquis ederit panem hunc indignè &c. Exploret autem quisque seipsum & edat de pane hoc. &c.
notes: 1 Cor. 11 Institution tropes; two things; stop §.V.
